author: reek
body: One program citing both transports, which is the thing that could not be written until `DtlsAction`'s `ActSend` became `ActSendFlight`.

author: reek
body: The collision was dormant rather than harmless. `Net chapter Tcp` declares `ActSend (List Integer)`, carrying bytes; `Encode chapter DtlsHandshake` declared `ActSend (Integer)`, carrying a flight number. Each chapter compiled alone and each chapter's own test passed, so nothing in the battery could see it -- a collision needs two citers in one unit to exist at all. Against the pre-rename chapter this file is `CDX3001: Duplicate constructor: 'ActSend' is already defined`, and no binary is emitted.

author: reek
body: That is what this test is: not an assertion about DTLS or about TCP, but the co-citation itself. It fails by not compiling, which is why it carries no `.failing` sidecar -- it is the positive case, and the negative was run by hand against the depot revision before the rename landed.

author: reek
body: Both arms are matched and both payloads are read, so the test also pins that the two constructors stayed distinguishable rather than one shadowing the other: a list of three bytes on the TCP side, flight seven on the DTLS side.
